name: Ferrite shield
description: A ferrite is a magnetically soft insulator: it carries no current, but its magnetic domains line up with a field and draw the field lines into it, so behind a ferrite plate a magnet's field is much weaker (a magnetic shield; electric fields pass, as through any insulator). The strong magnet behind the plate still nudges the beam a little. Place magnets to bring it into the detector.

reality.represents: Magnetic shielding by a ferrite plate

remarks.line: A soft magnet draws the field in
remarks.detail: A material of high permeability (μ = 1000) carries the field lines through itself, so beyond it the magnet's field is much weaker; electric fields pass, as through any insulator.
Its permeability is constant: no saturation (real ferrites saturate near 0.3–0.5 T), no hysteresis, no dependence on frequency; it is magnetized by the magnets and coils only.

A uniformly magnetized sphere has exactly a dipole's field outside it, which keeps the field simple and exact; real magnets are blocks, rings and pole pieces, and an instrument's magnet makes a field as uniform as it can.

Everything is symmetric about the plane z = 0, so the particle never leaves it. A real beam also has a width across the plane, where the same fields act differently (focusing in the plane can defocus across it).
